scene.label: Act 4, Scene 5
scene.title: SCENE V. Rossillon. A room in the Countess's palace.
scene.location: Rossillon. A room in the Countess's palace.

lines.text: No, no, no, your son was misled with a snipt-taffeta fellow there, whose villanous saffron would have made all the unbak'd and doughy youth of a nation in his colour. Your daughter-in-law had been alive at this hour, and your son here at home, more advanc'd by the king than by that red-tail'd humble-bee I speak of.

lines.text: I would I had not known him; it was the death of the most virtuous gentlewoman that ever nature had praise for creating. If she had partaken of my flesh and cost me the dearest groans of a mother, I could not have owed her a more rooted love.

lines.text: 'Twas a good lady, 'twas a good lady. We may pick a thousand salads ere we light on such another herb.
lines.plainText: 'Twas a good lady 'twas a good lady We may pick a thousand salads ere we light on such another herb

lines.text: Indeed, sir, she was the sweet marjoram of the salad, or, rather, the herb of grace.
lines.plainText: Indeed sir she was the sweet marjoram of the salad or rather the herb of grace

lines.text: They are not herbs, you knave; they are nose-herbs.
lines.plainText: They are not herbs you knave they are noseherbs

lines.text: I am no great Nebuchadnezzar, sir; I have not much skill in grass.
lines.plainText: I am no great Nebuchadnezzar sir I have not much skill in grass

lines.text: Whether dost thou profess thyself,—a knave or a fool?
lines.plainText: Whether dost thou profess thyselfa knave or a fool

lines.text: A fool, sir, at a woman's service, and a knave at a man's.
lines.plainText: A fool sir at a woman's service and a knave at a man's

lines.text: Your distinction?
lines.plainText: Your distinction

lines.text: I would cozen the man of his wife, and do his service.
lines.plainText: I would cozen the man of his wife and do his service

lines.text: So you were a knave at his service indeed.
lines.plainText: So you were a knave at his service indeed

lines.text: And I would give his wife my bauble, sir, to do her service.
lines.plainText: And I would give his wife my bauble sir to do her service

lines.text: I will subscribe for thee; thou art both knave and fool.
lines.plainText: I will subscribe for thee thou art both knave and fool

lines.text: At your service.
lines.plainText: At your service

lines.text: No, no, no.
lines.plainText: No no no

lines.text: Why, sir, if I cannot serve you, I can serve as great a prince as you are.
lines.plainText: Why sir if I cannot serve you I can serve as great a prince as you are

lines.text: Who's that? a Frenchman?
lines.plainText: Who's that a Frenchman

lines.text: Faith, sir, 'a has an English name; but his phisnomy is more hotter in France than there.
lines.plainText: Faith sir 'a has an English name but his phisnomy is more hotter in France than there

lines.text: What prince is that?
lines.plainText: What prince is that

lines.text: The black prince, sir; alias the prince of darkness; alias the devil.
lines.plainText: The black prince sir alias the prince of darkness alias the devil

lines.text: Hold thee, there's my purse. I give thee not this to suggest thee from thy master thou talk'st of; serve him still.
lines.plainText: Hold thee there's my purse I give thee not this to suggest thee from thy master thou talk'st of serve him still

lines.text: I am a woodland fellow, sir, that always loved a great fire, and the master I speak of ever keeps a good fire. But sure he is the prince of the world; let his nobility remain in's court. I am for the house with the narrow gate, which I take to be too little for pomp to enter: some that humble themselves may, but the many will be too chill and tender, and they'll be for the flow'ry way that leads to the broad gate and the great fire.

lines.text: Go thy ways, I begin to be a-weary of thee; and I tell thee so before, because I would not fall out with thee. Go thy ways; let my horses be well look'd to, without any tricks.
lines.plainText: Go thy ways I begin to be aweary of thee and I tell thee so before because I would not fall out with thee Go thy ways let my horses be well look'd to without any tricks

lines.text: If I put any tricks upon 'em, sir, they shall be jades' tricks, which are their own right by the law of nature.
lines.plainText: If I put any tricks upon 'em sir they shall be jades' tricks which are their own right by the law of nature

lines.text: A shrewd knave, and an unhappy.
lines.plainText: A shrewd knave and an unhappy

lines.text: So he is. My lord that's gone made himself much sport out of him; by his authority he remains here, which he thinks is a patent for his sauciness; and indeed he has no pace, but runs where he will.
lines.plainText: So he is My lord that's gone made himself much sport out of him by his authority he remains here which he thinks is a patent for his sauciness and indeed he has no pace but runs where he will

lines.text: I like him well; 'tis not amiss. And I was about to tell you, since I heard of the good lady's death, and that my lord your son was upon his return home, I moved the king my master to speak in the behalf of my daughter; which, in the minority of them both, his majesty out of a self-gracious remembrance did first propose. His highness hath promis'd me to do it; and, to stop up the displeasure he hath conceived against your son, there is no fitter matter. How does your ladyship like it?
lines.plainText: I like him well 'tis not amiss And I was about to tell you since I heard of the good lady's death and that my lord your son was upon his return home I moved the king my master to speak in the behalf of my daughter which in the minority of them both his majesty out of a selfgracious remembrance did first propose His highness hath promis'd me to do it and to stop up the displeasure he hath conceived against your son there is no fitter matter How does your ladyship like it

lines.text: With very much content, my lord, and I wish it happily effected.
lines.plainText: With very much content my lord and I wish it happily effected

lines.text: His highness comes post from Marseilles, of as able body as when he number'd thirty; he will be here tomorrow, or I am deceived by him that in such intelligence hath seldom fail'd.
lines.plainText: His highness comes post from Marseilles of as able body as when he number'd thirty he will be here tomorrow or I am deceived by him that in such intelligence hath seldom fail'd

lines.text: It rejoices me that I hope I shall see him ere I die. I have letters that my son will be here tonight. I shall beseech your lordship to remain with me till they meet together.
lines.plainText: It rejoices me that I hope I shall see him ere I die I have letters that my son will be here tonight I shall beseech your lordship to remain with me till they meet together

lines.text: Madam, I was thinking with what manners I might safely be admitted.
lines.plainText: Madam I was thinking with what manners I might safely be admitted

lines.text: You need but plead your honourable privilege.
lines.plainText: You need but plead your honourable privilege

lines.text: Lady, of that I have made a bold charter; but, I thank my God, it holds yet.
lines.plainText: Lady of that I have made a bold charter but I thank my God it holds yet

lines.text: O madam, yonder's my lord your son with a patch of velvet on's face; whether there be a scar under't or no, the velvet knows; but 'tis a goodly patch of velvet. His left cheek is a cheek of two pile and a half, but his right cheek is worn bare.
lines.plainText: O madam yonder's my lord your son with a patch of velvet on's face whether there be a scar under't or no the velvet knows but 'tis a goodly patch of velvet His left cheek is a cheek of two pile and a half but his right cheek is worn bare

lines.text: A scar nobly got, or a noble scar, is a good livery of honour; so belike is that.
lines.plainText: A scar nobly got or a noble scar is a good livery of honour so belike is that

lines.text: But it is your carbonado'd face.
lines.plainText: But it is your carbonado'd face

lines.text: Let us go see your son, I pray you. I long to talk with the young noble soldier.
lines.plainText: Let us go see your son I pray you I long to talk with the young noble soldier

lines.text: Faith, there's a dozen of 'em, with delicate fine hats, and most courteous feathers, which bow the head and nod at every man.
lines.plainText: Faith there's a dozen of 'em with delicate fine hats and most courteous feathers which bow the head and nod at every man
